I was only going to quote further, Mr. Speaker, in the event of the appetite of some of the ministers being whetted and wanting more. I have two choice ones here, but if it is not your wish, Mr. Speaker, that I shall read them, I will leave it at that. I have merely quoted these two paragraphs to show that my leader was quite justified in saying that the relation between the delegates of the mother country and Canada were strained, for here is a newspaper correspc-ndent who says the very same thing in very much blunter fashion.
I wish to deal for a short time with the conditions in agriculture. This is not a new subject, because during the three sessions previous to this the members from the west and from the east have repeatedly told the government of the gradually declining condition of our agriculture. I shall deal more particularly with western agriculture because I am not so familiar with the east as I once was. But I must say that I was very -much struck with a remark made by the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) yesterday. You would think she was describing conditions in the west instead of in the east when she said that she did not believe that there was a farm in Ontario that would be able to pay out of its revenues the cost of its operation and the taxes for the current year. No one ever knew of such a condition as that before in the history of Ontario or in the history of this country. We need only refer to the attitude of the mortgage companies towards agriculture. I remember that when I wras only the height of this desk, farm mortgages were thought to be gilt-edged, none better, good as the bank, and yet to-day I do not know of a farm mortgage company throughout the whole of Canada from Halifax to Vancouver that will lend one dollar on a farm mortgage. Why? Because farming is a non-paying, declining business, and the chances of getting your money back are too slim for the owner to let the money out of his hands on any farm mortgage.
In addition to that, the equipment of the farm is gradually declining. The hon. mem-

The Address-Mr. Motherwell
Der for South Battleford (Mr. Vallance) has already referred to that. Unless farmers are continually buying new equipment, the old will soon get into disrepair, the buildings and fences deteriorate, as well as everything else about the farm. The moment a farmer gets in that shape he cannot be an efficient farmer. The land begins to g-o down, and it will soon cease to bear the bountiful crops of other years. It gets weedy and out of condition. Why? Because the farmer cannot get back the cost of operating the farm out of the price he receives for his grain, with wheat at about thirty cents per bushel. There is a multitude of other difficulties, vicissitudes of one kind or another, because, as we know, troubles seldom come singly. We have gophers multiplying by the tens of thousands outside, and rats inside, in the barns, reproducing at a terrific rate. There are cut worms, winds and weeds and Tories galore, but in the dominion and in the provincial houses. The people feel that they are beset by all the plagues of Egypt, and some more. I think there were ten plagues of Egypt. One of them has not yet come to pass in the west. The rivers of Saskatchewan have not yet begun to run red, although a lot of people are seeing red. I do not think I am superstitious, but these things happened concurrently with the coming in of Toryism in this country after a long period of prosperous Liberal rule, and we cannot help wondering if there is not some connection between the two. Our minds go back to the fifteen years of prosperity under Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and to the eight or nine years of further prosperity under the King government, and our people are wondering if we will not have to have another change before things get better. Many hoped and 3ighed and prayed in 1930 for a change. Well, they surely got it, and now they are equally anxious for another change, and I think it is coming.
On the top of all these difficulties, we have the action of the relief commission, and this government must accept some responsibility for that. The Prime Minister said that they advised Saskatchewan to appoint a relief commission. They knew its personnel and they authorized them not only to make loans for relief and seed grain purposes to the farmers but supplied the money for it as well, and they authorized them-this is on the promissory notes and the seed grain liens -to collect the money on behalf of the Dominion government. So this government must accept some responsibility for the manner of collection. I must say that I have seen in Saskatchewan what I never expected

to see, and what never was done before to my knowledge. These loans were pressed for and are being pressed for by the relief commission, which endeavours to secure repayment on the very first crop after the sowing of the seed. I do not know of any other case like that in the whole history of Canada. It is true that in 1915, after the drought of 1914, the government of that day did start to make collections on the harvest of 1915. We had an enormous crop that year and the government were possibly justified in some measure in trying to collect some of these loans, but on the protest of the Department of Agriculture at Regina at that time that this practice should be discontinued at once, notwithstanding the big crop and the fair price which the farmers were receiving, that practice was discontinued. Por the farmers at that time to have attempted to pay the whole loan off in one year would have stripped them as bare of revenue as the day they were born. But today in every elevator throughout the relief areas you will find a list of names, and the elevator is asked to make collection as the farmer delivers his grain. There is no escaping it. Writh that bad example being set by the relief commission, and I warned the government what would happen if this course was pursued, we now see a great many of our municipalities doing the very same thing. What happened, for instance, in the old Indian Head municipality, where I delivered my grain for twenty years before a branch line was built north of it? For about ten years that was one of the largest initial shipping points in the world for wheat, a great wheat area, the home of the old Bell farm, the experimental farm and the forestry station. Two hundred and thirty out of three hundred farmers living in the municipality had their wheat seized for back taxes, as reported in the Regina Leader. Probably one of the reasons why some of the other seventy escaped was that they had threshed and sold their wheat before the distraint went into effect. Two hundred and thirty of them have only their wheat seed and grain to the value of $100, the report says, with which to face the coming winter. I learn that already the temperature has been as low as zero on the prairie, and if the temperature in the coming winter continues to increase in severity, those people will have difficult times. Many are quite unprepared for winter. However, that is the condition in which they find themselves. This government, through the relief commission at Regina, is collecting the seed grain liens only six months old, while private

The Address-Mr. Motherwell
creditors keep on waiting for years. If the government's present policy is pursued, half of those people will be back on relief before Christmas comes.
What has this government done for agriculture? Surely everybody recognizes that agriculture in Canada is a sick institution. Not only is it one of the leading industries, but it takes first place in the occupation of the majority of the peoples of the world. There are more people engaged in it than in any other vocation. In Canada, not quite 50 per cent of our population are farmers, but in the province of Saskatchewan a good deal more than that percentage are on the farms. One would have thought that such an important industry, one responsible for the feeding of the world, one representing more than half the population of the world, would have a little consideration at the hands of this government now, when it is sick unto death.
W hat is this government's record in connection with agriculture? One of the first indications we have is to be found in the wiping out of over S3,000,000 in agricultural estimates tabled last year. I should like to add that to build up agricultural estimates is not an easy matter. Some eight or ten years ago, sentiment around parliament hill was not very strongly in favour of the farmers. This was a political and social centre. But, agriculture-well, it was all right; of course it was necessary to have farmers to produce food for the urban communities. At that time, however, people on parliament hill did not attach as much importance to this industry as many of us thought should be attached to it, and that finally was attached to it before the late government went out of power. As a result of the activities of the Liberal government, estimates for agriculture went up higher than they had ever been before. The present minister, to his credit, raised them slightly in his first year. I think, however, that increase must have been a slip on his colleague's part; it must have been an accident, because it did not occur a second time. Then last session, at one fell swoop, the estimates were drastically cut. Never since the massacre of Glencoe, or Cawnpore at the time of the Sepoy outbreak has there been such a massacre as that which took place last year of the Department of Agriculture estimates. Through newspaper pressure, and from pressure within and without the house, over $800,000 of this was restored but this estimate is still over $2,000,000 less than in the year previous. That does not show a desire
to build up a sick agriculture. It looks like, having it down, they are giving it another shot in the eye. That is exactly what they did. The grants to the major winter and summer fairs were reduced by two-thirds of their former amount. The grant for the live stock pool, which was beginning to get on its feet and to function as an export institution, was reduced $10,000. This, plus eleven thousand dollars in losses sustained in exchange on the other side of the water put that institution out of the export business. That is the way the government is helping the farmers. Wonderful, wonderful! I wonder how long a patient would live if a medical doctor treated him that way; I wonder how long a medical adviser would be retained if he gave such service. Unfortunately, we can change our political doctors only once in four years, whereas a private citizen may change his doctor every day, if he so desires.
The hon. member for South Battleford (Mr. Vallance) made reference to machinery repairs. It is difficult to picture conditions in the country when farmers are attempting to take off their crop with old, dilapidated machinery. During harvest, time is precious, and one can imagine the exasperation of a farmei who has to run around the country and rely or his neighbour's junk pile for repairs when undei normal circumstances, he would be buying new machinery. Had the crops been big in some parts, I do not know how they would have harvested them because of defective equipment. How can they help it? They cannot buy new wagons because a new wagon box alone costs $40, and 120 bushels of wheat would be required to pay for it. I had occasion to buy -well, I did not buy it myself, but it was bought for me-a new inner garment, commonly known as a shirt. We had to give 27 bushels of rye for that shirt. That is a big load to carry around, and may I say if all my garments were bought anew with 15 cent rye it would take 503 bushels of rye to pay the bill. That would be a big jag of rye to carry-I mean of a solid nature.
This government first came to Ottawa in September, 1930, with cries of glee beyond imagination. They were as happy as though they had been going to a marriage feast. At that session they quadrupled the duties on farm implements and then gave the empty promise that the prices of that machinery would not increase. At first, repairs escaped this treatment, and we were asked to be grateful because they were left on the old schedule. That, in the first place, was an

The Address-Mr. Motherwell
admission that to have duties lowered was an advantage.
One would think that this government considered farmers a lot of children, that we had been in this life only two or three years, and knew nothing about affairs. One would think that they were of the opinion we did not know anything about the tariff fabrications they were spinning by the yard. Tariffs went up all along the line at that first special session. We will recall that when the house prorogued there was a brilliant display of gold braid, knickerbockers, gold buckles, and silk stockings, and all were eager to get to Quebec and across the water. Eight days after arriving in London an ultimatum was issued by the Canadian Prime Minister as to what should be done at the conference. Oh well, we will come to that in a few days. I just mention it by the way.
At the last session and the previous one, several matters were referred to the agriculture committee,-a proper place for matters pertaining to agriculture. Before that committee appear members of the staff of the department; experts are called; one may catechize them, and ask this, that and the other thing concerning the matter in hand. Of three important matters referred to the committee, two came from the Department of Agriculture, and one from the Department of Trade and Commerce. A great deal of evidence was heard, and all members of the committee were wondering as to where it would lead. A majority report was prepared, which came before the house, was read and tabled,- and then died on the roost. Whether or not the government were afraid to fight it through, I do not know. Whether or not they believe it was not worth fighting for, I do not know. I do know, however, that the effort in that committee, which ran nearly all session, was simply wasted and thrown away. Probably the committee reported something of which they were not sufficiently proud to ask concurrence in, anyway the report died on the roost and that was the end of it. Apparently no one can dare tell the truth about the condition of agriculture in this country except the Prime Minister, who sometimes tells it inadvertently. I have 'before me a statement made by the Prime Minister before the economic conference committee on monetary and financial questions. There is a good deal of it, but I wish to read only a few words:
Indeed it seems that new disequilibria are created almost as rapidly as old maladjustments are corrected-

These are the words of our Prime Minister, not a Jeremiah but one who is always optimistic.
-and the paralysis of business enterprise with profit margins uncertain or non-existent continues.
That is very different from the speech from the throne. Then the Prime Minister said:
Trade languishes and unemployment persists or tends to become aggravated.
The Prime Minister of Canada was the author of those words. No one can say anything from this side of the house without being dubbed a soap-box orator, a Jeremiah, a dispenser of nostrums or something like that, but the privileged individual who is the first minister of this country can say what he likes at the Imperial conference, spreading it all over the world, and that is all right. He was stating the actual facts of the case. I do not think one should go around advertising these things too much; I think as far as possible we should practise a certain amount of Coueism. I think the imagination has a good deal to do with the way we feel. Even if the sun obscures its face for a few hours we feel the effect upon our temperament; there is no question of that. I am sure my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Manion) will agree with me when I say that sick people are very much affected by their environment; that is why, when they go to the hospital, we send flowers, pleasant messages and hopes for recovery. But if a person has a broken leg that sort of thing will not cure it. In the same way, if your reserves are disappearing year by year, month by month and day by day, and you are getting to the point where you can see the finish not only of your reserves but of yourself, Coueism will not work under such circumstances and so that the government at some subsequent time may not say that we did not tell them of the condition, I am telling them now not for the first time but for the third or fourth time since this government came into power.
Last year the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) brought forward a proposal, not in the form of a bill but during the discussion of the estimates or the budget, relating to an export marketing board, and at that time I went almost beyond what was discreet in giving my sympathetic support to that proposal. I knew it would be quite unacceptable to the British people unless it was presented in a very diplomatic way, but I was prepared to give it a measure of reserved support if there was an ounce of possible help in it. I do not think some of my friends on this side

The Address-Mr. Motherwell
thought I was very wise in doing so, but that was the only opportunity I ever had to support a new proposal brought forward by the present government in regard to agriculture. Agricultural conferences have been held many times and policies have been advertised in the newspapers. Some of them have been repudiated by the minister, but I am afraid the records are against him. The information is all there; it can be found by anyone who wants to look in the records. In all this time, however, the only new policy brought forward had to do with the proposed export marketing board, but now we are told by the Imperial conference report that this proposal is up the flue also. A committee of the Imperial conference considered the question and decided that dumping duties and export marketing boards were not desirable, and they thought it would be better to wipe out the apparently three marketing boards which were already in existence than to create a further one here.
These are some of the things that the government has been doing presumably in aid of agriculture. Not one new policy has been instituted. Some good things have been done, but they have been copied from previous administrations dating back to Hon. Martin Burrell, and now the only new thing has been thrown on the junk pile. I think it might have worked if it had been taken up in the right way. I had hoped that perhaps the live stock pool would be resurrected; that would have been the first step necessary if the scheme had been carried through. The proposal to make the packers the medium for collecting a small charge from the producers of bacon as an export bonus was ridiculous; imagine anyone collecting the smallest possible charge on a three cent hog. They would be met with a pitchfork. That proposal was wisely discarded. There was another way in which this proposal might have been carried out, but since it has gone by the board we will not take time to discuss it. From this government we have not had one particle of new legislation worth a continental; so far as agriculture goes we have simply had the routine work being carried on. I may be wrong in that statement, but if anything else has been done I do not recall it. I will not dwell on what was attempted in connection with the world grain congress and some other things I might mention.
What is to be the future of agriculture, then, if it is in this condition at the present time, with equipment going down and no chance of replacing it at present prices? The only thing we can do is patch it up and keep going or, in the alternative, reduce our acreage to the 53719-15
capacity of our depleted equipment. We are entering upon a period when the law of the survival of the fittest will operate. All the misfits, the unfortunates, the aged, the inexperienced, the no-goods, and all kinds who through no fault of their own find themselves facing bankruptcy will have to drop out. We are often asked why we do not reduce our acreage in the west. The answer is that we would only make place for someone else. For many years the United States has been trying to reduce the acreage of wheat sown, but without success. The farmers take the ground that the other fellow will reduce, and then those who have not reduced will come along with a big crop at revived prices. The law of the survival of the fittest is one of the most inexorable, fearful, exacting and ruthless laws in the world. It is the law of the forest, of the jungle and of the wild life of the land, but I wonder if there is no other law for human beings. That, however, is the law that soon will be in operation. Very soon we will see a reduction of acreage on the open plains because of the inability of farmers properly to look after the land. Many farmers who today are operating a section of land are asking themselves if it would not be better to operate only three-quarters of that land, with their depleted equipment, rather than operate the whole section in an improper way. A half section well operated may give more profit than a whole section done at the wrong time in the wrong way. That is what the farmers are asking themselves, and I tell you that the law of the survival of the fittest, as well as the law of supply and demand, soon will be in ruthless operation on the plains of the west unless some miracle happens. Up to the present time practically all the acreage on the open plains has been kept in tillage, but that cannot continue much longer. I draw this fact to the attention of the government. It has started to nibble a little bit at tariff reduction in the conference agreements but it was only with reluctance and after great pressure had been brought to bear that certain duties were cut down. The government has not done nearly as much in this line as should be done, but maybe the spirit will grow, and more consideration will be given to agriculture. There is yet time to change from this ruthless exacting of high duties from the farmer, even on the repairs to his implements. The policy of this government seems to be to keep alive the secondary interests in the country even though that be done at the cost of the life of the primary industries. There is no reason why there should not be room



The Address-Mr. Motherwell
for both classes of occupation but if any preference is to be shown surely it should be to those who were first on the land and made necessary the secondary industries.
I believe my time has about expired and I must close even though the half has not been told. We on this side have been often accused of just railing at the government. I do not think the government is deserving .of any sympathy as long as its members, such as the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Sutherland), choose to wear out their chairs rather than stand up and wear out their boots by standing up and fighting. The government will have to take what is coming to it, that is all. I know the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) is quite capable of defending himself but apparently the fiat has gone forth from the bull moose of the Tory party that the best strategy is to keep quiet. That is the safest policy-the least said, the soonest mended.
I wonder if the following article which appeared in the Regina Leader-Post of September 30, will bring any member of the government to his feet. It reads:
Bennett Gave Party Funds
Contributed $750,000, says Turnbull in club address.
Prime Minister R. B. Bennett "placed $750,000 of his own money in our campaign funds and not much more than that was spent.
I question very much the latter part of that statement but no one has yet denied the first. I wonder if some hon. member on the government side will not get up-not in my forty minutes as was done in the case of the hon. member for South Battleford (Mr. Vallance) -and let us see what he looks like. The hon. member for North Huron (Mr. Spotton) is a good hitter; he can make black look white just as well as any other hon. member. If he cannot give an explanation, the rest might as well not try. Party funds have been discussed before in this chamber, in fact our own party has been under severe criticism. However, it must be remembered that according to the Prime Minister in a former debate there is not a member of this house who has not been assisted by campaign funds from the central committee. We are being told in effect, "Don't do as I do, do as I tell you; you must not have party funds, but we are going to have them. If we, the Conservatives, cannot get them any other way, our leader will dig them up." If some hon. member will get up we will have a snapshot taken as the one and only man in his party besides the Prime Minister, who has taken part in this debate.

If time permits I should like to make one or two suggestions. The first is that all the phases and branches of agriculture should be handled by one department. At one time the Department of Agriculture handled patents and copyrights and a number of other things which have since been turned over to the Department of Trade and Commerce. At one time wheat and all cereals were under the Department of Inland Revenue along with whiskies and tobacco. About thirty years ago they were transferred to the Department of Trade and Commerce, where they have since remained. Any hon. member who attended the meetings of the agriculture committee last year could not have helped observing the friction existing between two excellent staffs. I know of no other country where agriculture is handled by two ministers. That is not the logical and sensible thing to do, and in making that statement I do not criticize any past minister. The present Minister of Trade and Commerce may be better than any of the previous ministers, or vice versa, but that is not the question. No man or department can serve two ministers without breeding trouble.
My second suggestion is that the government should appoint a royal commission, first to diagnose the troubles that beset agriculture, and then to prescribe therefor.
Mr. E. C. ST-PERE (Hochelaga) (Translation: Mr. Speaker, my first thoughts are to extend my congratulations to the mover and seconder of the address. The hon. member for A'thabaska (Mr. Davies) spoke on behalf of the majority of the electors of his constituency and my good friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Laurin), devoted the greater part of his speech :n praising the personal accomplishments of the right hon. Prime Minister of Canada, a thing which nobody denies and who, I hope, if the praises of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier are deserved, will give our country an impulsion towards prosperity, and settle certain problems, which, unfortunately, under his administration, the country has not yet been able to solve. The speech from the throne is, so to speak, this session's program. It has many gaps and avoids broaching in a practical way, questions of the moment. Numerous speeches are delivered in the house of rather an academic character, and I wonder why one seems to avoid the problems which should call for our first consideration and require an immediate solution. The government, in the course of last session, had led us to believe that the unemployment question would present a more pleasing aspect, that this

The Address-Mr. St-Pere
anomaly would disappear with the tariff policy adopted and followed by the government. II is nothing new, but rather a truth of La Palice, to state that unemployment prevails, today, more extensively than last year, and, that the situation far from improving has reached the stage, where one oan say that Canadians not only feel the pinch of poverty, but that pauperism reigns supreme in all cities of our beautiful Canada. No doubt, we have all been a party, at least morally, to the methods followed, to this day, to relieve the poor and attenuate the distress of those who are despoiled of everything.
The dole has been a failure. Its distribution has not given the results expected, and we must at all costs try new means, if we wish to see a relative happiness return in the Canadian homes. The healers, sir, have not, for some time past, been scarce in this country; a new class of doctors, that have new remedies to cure this illness. First, they had recourse to the tariff. I put the question to you, sir, to this parliament and to all those desinter-ested, whether the tariff-regardless of the countries which apply it-has succeeded to attenuate the serious nature of the situation and improve business; and in the end given work to the unemployed who have spread over all our large cities. A rural member informed me at noon that the situation in his county was in all respect similar to that of large centres. These high tariff means are after all an exaggerated nationalism of which Lord Hugh Cecil made mention recently, in Europe, likening it to a devouring flame hindering all economic prosperity but especially all hope of financial restoration in all countries.
Others have thought it possible to remedy all the evil by appealing to social measures. I state, in all frankness, that this appeal to social measures has practically given no genuine results, up to date. As to Canada, the lack of uniformity of our social legislation, in the various provinces, is one of the great causes of the present situation. I wonder whether these great institutions that are so highly praised, such as the International Congress of Labour, the International Bureau of Labour, of which we hear so much, have succeeded in giving to the people of our provinces and to all our labour groups in Canada, the relief expected. I contend that these institutions have proved, up to now, to be of a truly European character, and that the labour question in Canada has been but slightly discussed. I have never, sir, appealed to the workmen of my constituency, as factory workers; I consider that all workers, whether in the intellectual sphere or in the mills, have
53719-15}
a right to an existence in our country; that the unemployed with a white collar, those having a profession and unable sometimes to collect their fees, the property owner, forced to lodge gratuitously his unemployed tenant, I state that all these various classes of citizens in Canada are entitled to some consideration from our institutions and are equally entitled to protection from the state.
"Talk" seems to be the main thing in this country. Why, faced with the distressing condition of the unemployed have we not attempted to enforce the scheme of Governor Winant, of New Hampshire? Why not have asked to gather, before a commission specially appointed to that effect, the representatives of our large financial organizations, manufacturers and working classes, so as to find out whether it would not have been possible to come to an understanding, either by a new division of the week and hours of work or by other means to relieve somewhat the present crisis. In our large cities, sir, the question of unemployment insurance is often raised. Speaking on behalf of the workmen of my constituency, workers accustomed in the past to find in our large mills remunerative wages, I state that this system of guarding against the consequences of unemployment finds no support among them. They ask for work, they request that society organizes itself to relieve them in a practical way. They recognize that it is a law established for centuries, that a person must earn his bread by the sweat of his brow, that a citizen must be thrifty, and must support his family. For all these reasons they do not look forward to becoming state pensioners, but demand that means be given to them so as to observe the commandment of daily work. Everybody lauds the precepts of all the great Christian organizations. The president of the United States and the Democratic candidate to the presidency, Mr. Roosevelt, recently commented, and this in a very praiseworthy manner, on the encyclicals of Pius XI; they quoted them as an example to the people of the United States. But if these sound conclusions, these admirable preambles of Christian economists, if these considerations emanating from the Vatican are so timely, what is the reason that those in authority, those who at present appeal for the people's support, do not immediately put them into practice. Public men necessarily seek solutions in political doctrines. With us, the government expects that a great improvement will result from the Imperial conference.
I shall not, sir, encroach on the debate which will take place next week on the sub-
The Address-Mr. St-Pere

ject. I shall limit myself to mentioning, to be in order, that certain impartial economists contend that nothing extraordinary will happen in Canada, as a result of the Imperial conference. The right hon. Prime Minister stated this week, that it would take four or five years before the good effects of the agreements concluded at the Imperial conference became apparent. What will become of the people in the meantime? This is, sir, the great problem which is thrust upon us. International coooperation and charity, well understood, in my opinion, are the only two means which might give genuine results after the next economic conference in London.
Much is heard about wiping out the war debts and disarmament. But, a very strange fact is that France is attached to her submarines, England to her tanks, Italy to her aeroplanes, etc. What is more extra-ordinaiy, the United States, that country so anxious for disarmament and which so strongly urges it on all Europe, to justify her relinquishment of war debts and loans to the allies, when the conference on disarmament was sitting, had her fleet of bombing planes perform evolutions over Mitchell Field and San Diego.
Let us now broach the subject of trade with Russia. I hardly took seriously, at the last session, the statement of principle of our friends opposite. We were asked, we Liberals, especially those of Quebec: Are you in favour or not of trade with Russia? As a matter of principle, no! But we were well aware that international trade often, if not always, pays little attention to questions of principle. And, this has just been proved. Russia indirectly carries on trade with Canada, and this can easily be explained. I hold an extract from the New York Times published last week and in which the following facts are mentioned: the international oil companies are very little concerned with the competition that Soviet Russia can carry on in trade throughout the world. They contend that such transactions have no political influence and foresee that they will have no specific effect on the price of oil as a whole. These foreign companies, states the article, are making a desperate effort to impress Moscow that the Soviet government cannot possibly remain alone in competing against all foreign countries.
Mr. Speaker, sometimes the representatives of the people are criticized for not keeping his electors well informed. In this house, as anywhere else, there are to be found partisans of "controlled economy" and other outside renovators who seek to do away with machin-

ery in order to relieve unemployment. I shall read an extract of an article published by Mr. Andre Liesse, the well known French economist, and in which are discussed these questions of "controlled economy," and the suppression of machinery, etc. I place on Hansard, knowing that it will dispel certain economic and social errors. The following is the extract of this important work published in the Economiste Francais.
Such is the case in industrial countries more particularly affected by the crisis. Hence come -in my opinion

budget difficulties. The economic depression lowers the tax returns and, there, where they weigh heavily, as in France, this additional financial burden increases the crisis. The improvident governments, swayed like their parliaments by the masses, have greatly contributed to this situation. Nobody is unaware of it, today. However, politicians responsible for the increases in the budgets, do not admit that they were wrong. They hope to entirely place the responsibility at the door of what some designate as "the anarchy of production." If the budgets do not balance, the reason is, that industry and commerce are not "controlled."
Controlled economy has, indeed, followers who harbour most pretentions notions. They wish to go to the root of the world's crisis. They advise as a remedy measures of intervention as old as those of taxes on the sale prices of food products and all commodities which sustain life. They acknowledge that the crisis is due to a too large production, taking into consideration the shrinkage of markets. They have somewhat abandoned the currency question, which at one time seemed to them of the utmost importance and was the object of their sole preoccupation. Machinery, the application of scientific discoveries to industry, worries them. A strange fact to note, the same discussions took place on the same word, more than a century ago; Sismondi has left us on "machinery" more thrilling pages than all those written, today, by the partisans of the "controlled economy."
They resort to the same arguments put forth by Sismondi, with the same error of judgment which the latter made during the industrial crisis which prevailed in England between 1818 and 1830. Sismondi had then to deal with a period almost violent in its technical evolution of industrial production. He thought the crisis would never end.
Those new inventions had thrown numerous workmen out of their jobs. Unemployment in England is a labour crisis which differs from the unemployment in other countries in that it is somewhat the sequel of the famous "Pauper Act" enacted to relieve pauperism and the result of which has been to maintain and spread it. Sismondi therefore concluded from facts he observed, that the introduction of machinery, in England, would lead, directly and irretrievably, the workman to pauperism.
In this he greatly erred as did Karl Marx who foretold, basing himself on a false doctrine, that social revolution would be provoked by the increasing distress of the workmen and wage earners, as a whole. Therefore, overproduction appears in the eyes of the partisans of the doctrine of "controlled economy" a

The Address-Mr. St-Pere
phenomenon which will continue-if it is not suppressed-to disorganize production and create anarchy in the economic world. What is, in their eyes, the true cause of the crisis? If we are to believe them, it is rationalization. But, rationalization manifests itself especially by the greater use of machinery. Machinery is therefore the main factor of the crisis. There is of course, beside machinery, properly speaking, organization-rational-of factories and staffs, also systematic work. This does not seem to disturb them, although the part played by the latter, also reduces the staff needed in enterprises. The trouble lies in machinery and they consider it the first cause of the crisis.
How are we to remedy this evil. We can hardly use repressive methods and punish inventors. For it was the very first method resorted to with great energy in the very early ages. Prometheus, the god of invention, was cruelly and longly punished. The necessities of war alone prompted Archimedes to make use of inventions on which he had worked. Petronius narrates that a Roman Emperor had the inventor of a light and malleable metal, which might have replaced gold and silver, put to death.
This proves that this preoccupation is not a new one. Although inventions continued to be looked upon with fear an attempt being made to smother them under the rule of corporations. Less than a century ago, Proudhon himself was much alarmed in seeing the spread of inventions. To guard against labour crises which they might create, he advised that machines and looms be placed in museums or in the "Conservatorie des Arts et Metiers-' to show the workman the new machines to be, by degree and wisely, introduced in mills and factories.
Today, we would have recourse to taxation to prevent or retard the application of scientific discoveries. The high priests of "controlled economy" would be the supreme judges of the necessity of using such and such machinery or such and such process in manufactures. With this system, the railway industry which replaced slow means of transportation, could not have made its appearance, it could not have laid its tracks or only made use by degree, of steam traction. And since it is a question of work and staffs employed, it is only necessary to compare the number of employees of railway managements with that of coaches to find out the truth. At present, the automobile is competing with railway transport. This is a question of fixing the rates of transport between the two systems. However, taxation must not be a medium of intervention to restrain the development of one industry _ of which those who would have full authority of "controlled economy" might fear the expansion. This is the socialist system. Thus to level fortunes and prepare the final revolution, taxation, while awaiting collective organization would serve to distribute wealth. One can imagine however, in connection with motor truck competition, more economical solutions of this problem could be found. It is probable that an understanding will be arrived at between the management of railways and companies of motor trucks on the bases of cooperation for the mutual advantages of both.
All these wrong notions have their source in the same conceptions. Those who adhere to them and wish to put them in practice, have
a belief and mystic faith in the economic and social power of the state. They do not think of the fact that it would be impossible for the men, chosen to look after the whole economic structure-for this must be the conclusion-[DOT] to fulfil this enormous task. Commissions and committees of experts would be appointed. One can foresee, by a few examples in the past, what would happen. Economic and social organizations are drawn on paper. Childish combinations are thought of which however, impress those who are unable to judge. What strikes us the most in these theories is that they prove among their authors a complete ignorance of the psychological and economic laws which have given us so many lessons since the war. It is true that one must be able to understand them.
The spreading of these theories contribute to the confusion of public opinion. They counteract the efforts of those who endeavour to enlighten this opinion. Never, perhaps, has it been more necessary to follow a sound policy of redress, and the latter must begin by convincing public opinion of the urgent requirements of the hour. We must immediately solve the public financial problems, balance the budget by sound means and not by expedients or doubtful trials. We must discover the true source of the evil. It will not be found in the scientific field of activities, or in their application, but in the errors made in the course of the post-war period and the crisis which it has created.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.
Mr. ST-PBRE (Translation): Mr. Speaker, the article which I read before we took recess can be applied to the present situation in a number of countries. Our financial liabilities are heavy to carry. Taxation has greatly increased. The provincial and municipal debts have reached more than a reasonable maximum. Property owners, but especially those who have been thrifty in order to provide for their old age, are at bankruptcy's door. The world seems completely upset. To obviate all these troubles, let us have recourse to international cooperation, let us refuse to. subscribe to all tariff policies of isolation, and let us not sign economic agreements equivalent to a new kind of zollverein. In the course of the speech delivered by Albert Thomas, at the Labour conference, presided by the hon. Senator Gideon Robertson, the ex-president of the International Bureau of Labour made the following remarks:
In tile face of all endeavours of social justice, this world crisis raises at every moment the question of economic possibilities. How, then seek the improvement of labour and living conditions of the working classes, without first establishing in the world economic and norma1 order?

The Address-Mr. Milchell
The International Organization of Labour, has not the means at its disposal to create this economic order. This organization is not vested with the authority to command. It must therefore turn to those who have such authority; towards governments and competent international institutions, and request them earnestly not to defer the measures which are necessary to restore political, financial, monetary and economic conditions, which will permit it, the International Organization of Labour, to carry out its task.
It is in this sense that the conference through the resolution voted, has made a touching appeal to the spirit of decision of the League of Nations and governments, in the hope of a prompt realization of the measures susceptible of relieving the present depression and thus realize the development of the work of social justice prescribed by the treaties of peace.
Labourers and artisans of all classes, financiers and industrialists will find in a sound economic and social understanding the return to that prosperity that an egotism of low standard and the high tariffs have set aside for some years past. The salvation of nations, sir, rests in their interdependence well interpreted by those who have been given the mission to guide them.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire at this time to make a few observations on the speech from the throne. I think the speech itself might be likened to the maiden's prayer, it relies more on hope than on positive action. But it absolutely misses the vital problem confronting the people of this country, the problem of unemployment. At the last general election it was generally understood that the leader of the present government said that his government would cure unemployment or perish in the attempt. The perishing at the present time is being done by the hearers rather than tby the gentleman who made that undertaking. I am inclined to agree with a member who spoke previously in this debate, that the government should carry out its solemn obligation to the people and meet them in conformity with the promises made in the last election.
The leader of the government also made another observation in connection with soap box orators who were going up and down this country. If he does not know I would like to tell him that the leader of the government in Great Britain, Mr. Ramsay MacDonald, owes his rise to political power to the fact that he was once a soap box orator. The same might be said of Philip Snowden,

of J. H. Thomas, and of many other men who have reached eminence in the public life of the mother of democratic institutions. I do not know any better way of feeling the pulse of the people in this country than by going out and meeting them, even though it should be on a soap box. I am of the opinion that possibly even the Prime Minister of this country might have a better grasp of national problems as they affect the daily lives of the men and women engaged in agriculture and industry, he might have closer contact with them, had he early in his career done some soap-boxing himself. I appreciate the fact, speaking from experience, that the life of a soap box orator is not a very happy one. You are asked some very awkard questions at times whilst discussing the problems that affect your constituents. It might be well if the government of the day did a little soap-boxing and got away from this city, because after all is said and done the city of Ottawa is something like Rome and Athens, it is drawing tribute from the rest of the country. I do not say that in any critical sense, but it is a fact that must be recognized that to get a true picture of the problems and conditions confronting the people it is absolutely necessary to get out among them.
The first matter dealt with in the speech from the throne was that of the agreements arising out of the recent Imperial conference. I appreciate that they will be a subject for discussion during next week, but I would like to say this regarding them, and the approach to the very vital problems in connection therewith. It must be remembered that with possibly one exception previous Imperial conferences dealt with the legal status of the colonies or dominions as the case might be. In fact they were largely taken up with, might I say, a philosophical discussion of abstract legal questions. They ratified declarations that were generally in effect before the ratification took place. In connection with the recent conference, you have an entirely different set of facts to face. I am not at all worried at the stories you hear about scraps inside the conference. That is only human nature. I have been in many conferences over wages and working conditions, and though our problems were settled satisfactorily, we did not always get through those conferences without very deep differences of opinion. There is, however, one

The Address-Mr. Mitchell
lesson which I think the country might well take to heart; I hope that in future we shall not have the same amount of ballyhoo and the expectations raised in the minds of the people that we had in connection with the recent conference. If you have trade agreements to negotiate, it is far better to negotiate them in a calm spirit, somewhat after the manner in which the Australian agreement was negotiated in Honolulu, or the New Zealand agreement; because do not forget that Great Britain lost the American colonies over questions of trade and taxation. These are very delicate questions.
The agreements reached at the recent conference are in principle protectionist. They merely divert trade from avenues that have been built up, and notwithstanding the deep study that is being given to the schedules at the present time, it is absolutely impossible to pass judgment upon them until such time as the attitude of other nations in regard to them has been learned. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that we are in for a period of what I might call international starvation, with restrictions being placed by one nation upon another, and in an effort to overcome those restrictions the various countries of the world are driving down the living standards of their working people and agriculturists. That is a fact which in my judgment we in this country should clearly recognize in our approach to the problems that confront the men and women of this Dominion.
The next important matter in the speech from the throne of concern to the labour men and women of this country is the position of the railways. It must be remembered that the transportation commission sat at a time when we were in the throes of an acute depression; had it been possible for us to obtain the observations of these commissioners in 1929, they might have been entirely different. The direct question might be asked of some of the members who sat on that eommisison, particularly those who are officers on other roads, what is the condition of their own roads? Do they not need commissions to look into them just the same as we found a transportation commission necessary in this country? I readily understand that major economies are thought necessary, but I would point out that these economies
are going to fall upon the shoulders of the men engaged in that particular industry. We are to have economies put into operation for the purpose of doing away with duplication of services. It is in keeping with the spirit of the times, in municipalities, in governments, federal and provincial, and in industry, to lay off the men and women engaged in these various institutions and industries in an effort to get from under. If that is deemed necessary in connection with the railways, I believe it would be well to pause a little until conditions are nearer to normal-if they are ever to return to normal-because it must be remembered that men who have spent the best part of their working life in the railroad industry, and who are experts in their particular job, will be thrown out of work to swell the ranks of the unemployed. Every man and every woman who is laid off in industry and commerce creates a problem in relation to their buying power in industry and commerce.
I was pleased to hear the observations of the right hon. leader of the opposition to the effect that labour should be represented on the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways. I do not know anybody who has more interest in the success of this great undertaking than the labour men themselves, and I believe that in the ranks of labour in this country there are men just as able to supply the directing force, and at the same time lend that human touch that we believe is essential, particularly in these days of acute depression, as can be found anywhere else.
So far as the St. Lawrence deep waterway is concerned, the constituency I represent is deeply interested in seeing this project become an accomplished fact. We believe that the forty millions of people who live around and in the vicinity of the great lakes should be given access to salt water. While in the navy it was my experience to travel extensively in many parts of the world. I found that where there are ample facilities for ocean navigation, development is advanced. In my judgment, transport by water is, and will continue to be, the most economical form of transportation. Apart from the money it will put in circulation, the much needed employment it will give to men out of work, and the added supply of power which will necessarily quicken the development of the eastern section of Ontario, I believe this project will promote
The Address-Mr. Mitchell

A summary indicates that in one week of 1931 there were 2,446 families on relief, costing the city $11,921.39, while in the corresponding week in 1932 there were 5,153 families on relief, costing the city $24,929.06.
My time is drawing to a close, Mr. Speaker. I did intend to quote from this very able study of relief measures in Ontario by Mr. Cassidy of the University of Toronto, but I have not time. I do believe, however, that unless there is some change in the very near future many municipalities throughout this Dominion will face bankruptcy. The present condition cannot go on. Our sources of taxation are so limited that we will have to receive greater assistance from the federal and provincial governments throughout the country.
In conclusion I should like to state that we are passing through a war, and I think everyone will admit that we are in retreat. Against us we have ranged the driving force of science expressed in mass production, and those people who insist on adopting the policy of sticking their heads in the sand must face the facts. That attitude is expressed in the following words contained in the speech from the throne:
The unity, fortitude and capacity of the Canadian people, without which all your labours would have been in vain, shall be now the foundation upon which, with cooperation and faith, we will build a Canada greater than we have yet known.

Mr. Speaker, my first word will be one of congratulation to the young man from my province who moved the address in reply to the speech of His Excellency the Governor General (Mr. Davies). While the hon. member is not of my political persuasion, nevertheless I am pleased that he shows promise. His speech was carefully prepared; it needed a little more enlightenment upon fiscal matters, but he may yet prove to be a creditable representative from our province. I wish also to congratulate the seconder of the address (Mr. Laurin), another young man of some promise. However, I must express the same regret as has been expressed by other speakers who have preceded me, that he and his colleague find themselves in their present company. Perhaps they may see the light at some future date and move across the floor of the chamber into the environment in which they belong.
I am entirely in accord with the remarks of my hon. leader (Mr. Mackenzie King). He spent considerable time in reviewing the actions of this government. While that review was comprehensive and covered a great deal, there are still many things which have been left unsaid with respect to this administration.
In replying, the leader of the government (Mr. Bennett) made his usual type of speech. I have read his speech with some care but I cannot discover any justification of the results obtained by his government. The results speak for themselves. If one had the time he could enumerate the many acts of this government since its inception and show that each has had disastrous effects. It has been a case of hasty action and just as hasty withdrawal. As far as I can discover, not a single act of the government commends itself as being in the public interest.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I had not intended to refer to that, but may I say to my hon. friend-

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

speechtext:
It is eight or ten days since we assembled in this chamber for the opening of the session, and we have had almost complete silence on the part of my hon. friends opposite. That silence cannot be because of a lack of criticism from this side of the house, particularly of domestic import.
The whole administration of this government has been in direct contradiction of its promises. Take unemployment, for instance. Did the members of the government not go from one end of the country to the other and proclaim in clarion tones that if they were placed in a position of authority, unemployment, which had become a national question, would be taken care of? The other day my hon. leader gave quotation after quotation from the statements made by the Prime Minister. In 1930, the Prime Minister in his own city deprecated the fact that unemployment was so rampant in this country and stated that if given the opportunity he would set up machinery to take care of it. Then he goes back in 1932, two years afterwards, and tells the assembled premiers of the provincial governments and the mayors of the cities of western Canada that unemployment is not primarily the responsibility of the federal government-a direct reversal of the clear-cut statement previously made to his own electors. How can anyone have confidence in hon. gentlemen who make definite statements on one occasion and then shortly afterwards take exactly the opposite position?
Then, adding insult to injury, the Prime Minister states that if it had not been for the leader of the opposition and hon. members on this side there would have been no interference with the progress of the Imperial conference.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
An hon.
member says, "hear, hear," but I challenge hon. gentlemen opposite to name one occasion when any member of the Liberal party, from the leader down, said a word other than to hope that the conference would be a success. It ill behooves the leader of the government

The Address-Mr. Stewart (Edmonton)
to throw such a challenge across the floor at the leader of the opposition, who has been most sincere in his desire that the conference should be a success. Hon. gentlemen opposite would like the impression to go abroad that obstacles have been placed in the way of the success of this conference. The agreements have been consummated and no obstacle can be put in their way. We have had an opportunity of perusing their provisions and later will have a chance to discuss them in their entirety.
In 1930 it was considered a terrible catastrophe for this country to have one hundred thousand unemployed. At that time it was stated that this condition of affairs was the direct responsibility of the Liberal government and its followers. What were the gentlemen across the way going to do should they be put into power? They were going to cure unemployment or perish in the attempt. It would have been a godsend if every one of them had perished long ago.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
They have not even made
an attempt.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I want hon. members to understand that I mean perish politically, not physically. What has the government done?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Nothing.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
My hon.
friend says "nothing." The tariff has been increased to an unprecedented degree; industry has been stifled and in many instances destroyed; unemployment has increased to an extent never witnessed before. Hon. members opposite say that this is because of world conditions. We said that in 1930, and hon. gentlemen opposite went out to their electors with the statement that in a young country like Canada, with its natural resources still undeveloped, there was no reason for unemployment provided the government did its duty. Let this government do its duty in the light of the statements made on that occasion. Those statements cannot be denied and the government stands condemned and convicted of having misled the public as no government has ever done in the past.
I wonder if those hon. gentlemen who have got into the seats of the mighty and are in easy circumstances these days ever go out and mix with the unemployed. I invite them to go to western Canada, but if they cannot accept my invitation I will tell them what they would see tonight. They would see men sitting around a fire made of a few sticks of wood; men with no place in which they
can find shelter except in what is known in western Canada as Canadian Pacific pull-mans-the freight cars. Not one, not dozens but thousands of them, honest, intelligent, educated men sit around with tin cans and with insufficient clothing to keep themselves warm. It would rend the heart of any man who has any human sympathies to see what is taking place in the country today; and yet the leader of the government makes not a single attempt to provide assistance apart from what he himself condemned in the most emphatic terms in his own city of Calgary, namely, the dole. He offers no other provision, makes no other effort for alleviating unemployment, apart from the dole or direct relief as he is pleased to call it. That is all the sympathy he has with the seven or eight hundred thousand men and women in this country. That is all the sympathy they get from the government of the day occupying the treasury benches. If that is not an indictment of inefficiency and incompetence then I do not know what sort of indictment one would lodge against them. They said that they would call a special session and would increase the tariff in order to create employment, and that they would build up industries in this country. And. mark you, the great natural resources of Canada were at their disposal. These same gentlemen the government of the day, before they came into office, stated that if these natural resources were utilized there need be no unemployment, but that there would be work for all-work, not doles. Yet they sit there impotent and helpless, convicted on their own statements of being the most useless government that Canada has ever seen.
What about the tariff? The tariff was going to cure all our ills. Not satisfied with their majority, with which they could pass legislation of any description, and will pass, of course, despite what anyone may say, not satisfied with that authority, they wrest authority from parliament itself so that it may be exercised by the executive, unhampered; and duties are pyramided until we have, not protection, but exclusion in Canada. And they wonder why unemployment is increasing. They have penalized the farmers of this country to such an extent that it will take years for them to recover. Let me say, Mr. Speaker, that the farmers of Canada today have no illusions whatever of what is being done to them. All they want is an opportunity to go to the ballot box and they will deal with these hon. gentlemen in the only way that they will understand.
Consider what the tariff has done to western Canada. Owing to the imposition of ex-
236	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Stewart (Edmonton)
cessive tariffs that keep the spread between primary and secondary industries so great, foreign markets where we formerly sold our produce are now closed to us, so that we can sell neither our wheat nor our cattle; we cannot sell our mineral products nor anything else. The result is that you have fifty per cent of the population of Canada, engaged in agriculture, without markets; and these producers must have markets wide and varied if they are to exist. You must, of course, purchase if you are going to sell; but hon. gentlemen opposite say, "We will not purchase anything; we will not allow anything to come into Canada for consumption if there is the remotest possibility of its being manufactured in this country." Well, what has happened? I was talking to a senator from New Brunswick today, and may I observe in passing that some gentlemen from New Brunswick have been quite vociferous in defence of the Tory party. This gentleman is not a Liberal, and he told me, when I discussed with him farm conditions in western Canada, about the state of affairs in New Brunswick. He said, "You in the west are no worse off than we are in New Brunswick, because in the oldest rural settlements down there the farmers find themselves in a very serious position. They are unable to sell their products, and conditions are so bad that we have to deny the children of our community educational facilities, because we have to close our schools." What a nice thing for hon. gentlemen opposite to contemplate. That is the way their policies are working out.
When the Prime Minister said to the provincial premiers and the mayors of municipalities in the west, "Unemployment is primarily your responsibility," they should have retaliated by saying, "Yes, that may be; but your policies with respect to trade restrictions have aggravated this problem to such a degree that it is becoming unbearable, and if you persist in carrying out these policies you must take the responsibility for the consequences of your administration." There are some rights that belong to the provinces. What have tariffs done to the western farmer, Mr. Speaker? All you need to do is to go to the west and take up any newspaper, and what do you see? At least forty per cent of all lands are in the municipalities, and those are not municipalities that were stricken by drouth but municipalities in which there have been reasonably decent crops during the past few years. What is the situation to-day? These places are for sale for taxes.

speechtext:
Yes, by
recent provincial governments. The hon. member who interrupts was a member of the legislature in the days when we attempted to keep taxation within reasonable bounds, and I heartily agree with him that there has 'been an C'i'gy of expenditure there, totally unwarranted, as well as on the part of every other provincial legislature of Canada. But we are not discussing provincial legislatures just now, nor are they responsible for unemployment. When you deny the individual on the land the right to receive a decent return for his labour, when you do so by means of federal legislation, there can be only one result, and we see it to-day not only in the west but throughout Canada. The greatest agency for socialism in Canada to-day sits right over there. He will socialize the land of Canada to an extent that no one has ever anticipated. Yet hon. gentlemen hold up their hands in holy horror at the idea of communism or socialism. In the west to-day over thirty per cent of real estate in the city belongs to the municipalities, and if this continues in the rural municipalities it will not be very long until over fifty per cent of the lands will be in the hands of the rural municipalities. Is that socializing land? I charge this government and the leader of the government with having, by the vicious legislation which they have enacted in connection with the tariff, brought about that state of affairs.
I believe implicitly in private ownership and in freedom, and I am alarmed at the rate at which this process is going on. What else have they done? Another instance of the way in which they are socializing Canada is to be seen in the fact that by the imposition of these high tariffs, by the closing of avenues of trade, they are obliged to increase taxation. The Minister of Finance is a good friend of mine and I am sure his head must be aching. I sympathize with him in the task he has undertaken, for it is not a pleasant thing to have to come to parliament time after time and admit that the budgeting of the government does not bring the expected results. May I say to him that so long as he supports his leader in the imposition of these impossible duties, stifling trade, he will be in that unfortunate and unhappy condition. May I say to him that the policies of this government are a direct reversal of the

policies that were put into effect by the Liberal party in 1922 and which brought about such happy results. After nine years we were able to point with some pride to the fact that we had reduced taxation, and we had reduced the public debt by $273,000,000-

There is
no objection, Mr. Speaker, let them interrupt. But what is the condition today with respect to taxation. At every session of this parliament, and I suppose it will be repeated this session, we have had to increase taxation. It has been increased, I figure roughly, to the extent of some $40,000,000 already, and they have increased the public debt. Hon. gentlemen need be under no misapprehension; the railway has nothing to do with this. They have increased the public debt of Canada by $200,000,000. Quite a creditable record, isn't it? May I say this, and say it in all sincerity: it does not lie within the province of hon. gentlemen opposite to criticize the administration of the Canadian National Railways, for this government has gone into debt even faster than they did. Hon. gentlemen on that side sit smugly back and criticize the Canadian National Railways, that did not, when all is said and done-and I have not been an exponent of the Canadian National Railways-did not run into debt any more swiftly than the government which sits on the treasury benches today.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: What about the two billion dollars you added to the Canadian National Railway debt?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Two billion dollars covers their whole debt. My hon. friend must be very badly informed. The rate at which hon. gentlemen opposite have increased taxation owing to the policies they have adopted with respect to the tariff can lead to only one end; how long can the people of this country stand that kind of thing? Hon. members have heard the record of the city of Hamilton, of the city of Toronto, of the city of Montreal. These are eastern cities; they are not the cities that hon. gentlemen opposite are so fond of complaining that we westerners come from continually bewailing our difficulties. No; the difficulties have struck the party opposite, and if they are honest and sincere and willing to tell the truth about the matter, they will admit they are thoroughly disturbed about the situation, as any thoughtful man must be.
May I say this one word about the provisions of the new agreements? There are more increases in tariffs-twice as many increases as decreases, as far as I can discover. And they do not in any sense compare with the favourable position that Great Britain occupied in the Canadian market prior to
1930.	Protection? Why we have protection gone mad. Exclusion? Yes, in the hope that it would benefit industry. And you have industry throttled and stifled, you are crucifying agriculture in every part of Canada. What a beautiful record of administration! It is little wonder that you have turned dumb and are afraid to defend it.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: We are reaping what you sowed.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
God help
you when you come to reap your own crop! Mr. Speaker, if there was one single ray of light in connection with this administration we would have seen it. But there really is none. And the most tragic part of it all is what it entails in human suffering and misery. The loss in money does not mean so much. In war time we said that our regrets were not for the money spent but for the human suffering and loss which the conflict entailed. May I say to hon. gentlemen opposite that two more years of their administration will leave a trail perhaps as disastrous financially and in human suffering as the war left upon Canada. They may regard these as strong
238	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Stewart (Edmonton)
statements, but think them over for a few moments; 750,000 men and women unemployed in Canada tonight. That is the registered unemployed; you can easily multiply that by two so as to take in the unemployed who are living upon their friends or their parents. I have a son at McGill university this year, and he was the sole student in his class who received employment. What were the rest of them doing? Not a single thing. Yet, how these gentlemen used to declaim about bringing the boys back from the United States and giving them employment in Canada! And they have to admit that there is not a job for any young man coming out of an educational institution today in Canada. If there is a job at all he has to give place :o some unfortunate married man with a wife md family to support.
The leader of the government went throughout Canada deploring the fact that widows and orphans were suffering, and he could not bear to see them suffer. I wonder where he is tonight. I wonder how he feels about it now, when the number is at least ten or fifteen times what it was in days when he was so solicitous about unemployment. When will he discover, and when will hon. gentlemen opposite discover where this suicidal policy that they are pursuing is leading them? All they say, through the mouthpiece of their speaker, the Prime Minister, is "Thank God, we are not so badly off as other nations are." Well, Mr. Speaker, I for one do not believe that there is any occasion for the extent to which unemployment has gone in this country. I charge the government with being directly responsible for the present situation. I do not say that the depression can be entirely blamed upon this government; no one will say that. It is world-wide in its extent. Every trading nation in the world of any importance thought that it was going to cure its difficulties by raising tariff barriers and preventing exchange of goods, and every one of these nations is in a similar position to that in which Canada finds itself. Has one hon. gentleman opposite an original idea for curing the present evils? Ai they can do is copy what other nations have done, and that is why our position is what it is today.

speechtext:
What about free
trade England?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Hon. gentlemen opposite should nolt say anything about England, because they have brought this country into a position where it is ten times worse off than England, and have done that

within a period of less than twenty-four months. That is their record, and if 1 were in itheir shoes I would not say very much about conditions in England. If hon. gentlemen opposite have nothing constructive to suggest, then for heaven's sake let us get busy on the dole and do something for suffering humanity, for our own kith and kin in Canada.
But, Mr. Speaker, there are other ways of curing unemployment. I say, give these unemployed men work rather than doles. Change your fiscal policy and you will put one-half of them into employment in lose than six months, and the remainder will very soon be taken care oif in productive employment. But you will not do it. You will persist in this insane policy of protection which is destroying the vtery industries you seek to protect. The number employed in secondary industries in this country is not so great. We had about 800,000 people employed in secondary industries when this government took office, and now we have 800,000 out of employment, and a large proportion of them were engaged in secondary industries.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
There would have
been millions out of work if you had been in power.
