subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hon. members must not address each other. That is unparliamentary. They must address the Chair.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
May I say, Mr. Speaker, that I am always delighted to address the hon. gentleman who now occupies the position of Speaker in this chamber.
In conclusion, much as I dislike supporting policies of hon. gentlemen apposite, may I say that if they will introduce measures that will have a practical effect in reducing unemployment, they will have my hearty support. So far as the Imperial conference agreements go in that direction they will have my hearty support; but so far as they go in the opposite direction they will meet with just as vigorous opposition. That is my position, and I am not speaking for the Liberal party; 1 am speaking for the hon. member for West Edmonton. There is no excuse for the situation in which we find ourselves today, with 800000 men unemployed, and with taxation increased to an unheard-of degree. 1 do not know what Ithe Minister of Finance will tax further, but I do know that he will have to get more revenue. Every time that he puts on a tax and hopes to get some revenue, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ryck-

The Address-Mr. McPhee
man) contrives to have an order in council passed thait prevents the anticipated revenue coming into the coffers of the country. No one can deny that the record of this government is that in two years it has increased the indebtedness of Canada by $200,000,000; that it has greatly increased taxation, and that unemployment is now wide-spread to an unprecedented degree. Is not that a splendid record of achievement by a group of individuals who have the responsibility of administering the affairs of Canada at this time?
I am amazed that some of the independent members of the Conservative party from the good old province of Ontario can sit quietly in their seats and put up with this kind of thing. I often wonder what happens in the quiet of their rooms upstairs. I should not like to use in public-I suppose it would not be allowed-the language which they must use in private, because I have some conception of the feelings of hon. gentlemen opposite. Throughout this debate they sit absolutely dumb. Possibly their hope is that when the provisions of the Imperial conference agreements are under discussion they will be given an outlet for their views. I do hope that they are given an opportunity then, because it is a terrible predicament for them to be in, to be sent here as representatives of the people and then to sit silent through the session without the opportunity of expressing themselves. Every announcement is made by the leader of the government himself on behalf of the 136 members who sit behind him, and when he finally turns around and says, as he did on one occasion, "Now you boys get up and vote,"-well, I have heard the Prime Minister on many occasions make the statement, "What a spectacle!"- and I can only say to him and to hon. gentlemen opposite when I think of them in that position: What a spectacle!
May I plead with hon. gentlemen opposite to do something constructive? Surely by this time they must have realized the utter im-potency of the remedies that they have applied. Surely they must realize it is time for them to right about face and adopt some of these Grit doctrines that they have decried on any and every occasion. Let them just try out those doctrines and see if they will not do something to cure the unenviable situation in which Canada finds itself to-day. That is my advice-take it or leave it. But if they take it I promise, irrespective of what other members of my party may do, that I will give such proposals my hearty support.
Mr. GEORGE W. McPHEE (Yorkton): Continuing the discussion on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, my first duty, in common with others, is to compliment the mover (Mr. Davies) and the seconder (Mr. Laurin) for the splendid presentation they have made of the case so far as the government of the day is concerned.
We have listened all this week, Mr. Speaker, to a terrific indictment preferred against the government of this country without one, single, solitary member supporting the government getting up in its defence. Some of us have sat patiently in the expectation that the western members who are supporting this government from the province of Saskatchewan, for instance, would rise in their places and approve or disapprove of the indictment which we have preferred against this government so far as western Canada is concerned. But as they have not disapproved of it, I presume that they are willing to take credit for the conditions that exist in Saskatchewan and throughout Canada today.
Canada, Mr. Speaker, like a great many other countries of the world, is suffering. We have an abundance of wheat. In the United States they have an abundance of cotton. There is an abundance of coffee in Brazil, an abundance of rice in China, an abundance of wool in Australia, and yet peeple throughout the world are starving, perishing, simply because they have not got these commodities. What is the reason? It is not a matter of overproduction; it is a matter of underconsumption. Why are not people in the rest of the world consuming these goods? Simply because they have not the wherewithal to buy them, and they are prevented by unsound tariff barriers from getting goods into circulation. There is not an economist of note in the world today but stresses that statement. I have read the views of Sir Arthur Salter, Sir George Paish, Professor Einzig, of the University of Paris, and Professor Soddy of Oxford university. These men, economists of high standing, all sound the warning that unless this world gets away from unsound tariffs, destruction will be the result.
Perhaps I may be permitted to place on record a few lines by Sir George Paish. Listen to this indictment:
The outlook of the statesmen now in control of the world's destinies with their historical background is undoubtedly a survival of the mentality of the statesmen who direeted the affairs of nations in the days when the world was in its infancy, and when countries were compelled by physical and other obstacles to be practically self-contained.
The Address-Mr. MePhee

And again.
Finally, the weight of the evidence proves conclusively that the nations one and all, cannot recover their prosperity or enter upon a new period of expanding well-being until trade between them is permitted to flow with complete freedom.
Then again,
All experience indeed proves that the road to prosperity runs in the direction of encouraging every nation to produce the commodities for which it is specially gifted and to exchange its products freely for those, whether raw or manufactured, which other nations are specially qualified to produce, and that just in proportion as this exchange takes place, trade expands and the standard of life throughout the world rises to higher levels. It is the disregard of this principle and the effort which the nations are now making again to become self-contained, that is bringing them to an extremely perilous position.

What has been the attitude of this government to the farming population? It cares nothing whatever for the farmers, the great producers of the land. That always has been the history of the Tory party. Let me verify that statement. In 1911 a delegation of a thousand farmers came down from western Canada to interview t.ho government of the day. At that time there was a stalwart Conservative in the house by the name of bii Sam Hughes. Page 7134 of Hansard of 1910-11 contains the following words of his which have never been denied or contradicted by members of the Conservative party:
Why sir, you would actually think it was this gang of leaders; this grain growers association from the northwest that came down here, the same sort of fellow we find popping up in blacksmith-shop statesmanship. Everyone of them -a Grit organizer and heeler; not the rank and file of the farmers of Canada, but the men who try to push themselves _ to the front and whose wives are at home wearing long boots and cleaning out the cow stables and the horse stables, while these fel ows are hanging around the blacksmith shops spouting statesmanship for the world over.
That is the record of the Conservative party as far as the fanners of this country are concerned. That is Toryism with a vengeance. But is that much worse than the treatment meted out to the farm delegation which came down to this fair city a few months ago? At least Sir Sam Hughes had the courage of his convictions, he got up in the house and said so. What about the Prime Minister of this country? What about the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) from western Canada, the back-bencher occupying a front position? Where was he on that occasion? Why did not he or some other member of the government come down and interview that delegation?
In 1930 the leader of the government stated that the tariff was to be the cure-all, that his

party was going to bring the farmer out of the wilderness with that means. I remember the elections very well. My opponent went even one better than the Prime Minister. He stated that the farmers of western Canada were not getting as much for their butterfat as they should be getting for their buttermilk, and said: "Put my leader in power and you will receive as much for your buttermilk as you are getting now for your butterfat" What are the facts? Never before in the history of Canada have prices been at such a low level as they are at the present time.

The price of farm machinery has not gone down as much as it would have had the tariff been reduced and not increased. So much for that phase of the subject.
I shall now deal briefly with the sub-amendment moved by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote). At the outset I will state that I am in sympathy with the principle of this amendment. There is no doubt that to-day the concentration of the wealth of the world is in the hands of a very few people. Next to the tariff, this concentration is largely responsible for the condition in which we find ourselves. This afternoon the hon. member for South Battleford (Mr. Yallance) read an extract from Thomas Carlyle which had been written about one hundred years ago. I should like to quote a statement by the same writer which might well have been written today. It reads:
Wealth has accumulated itself into masses, and poverty also in accumulation enough, lies impassably separated from it opposed uncommunicating like forces in positive and negative poles. The gods of this lower world sit aloft on glittering thrones less happy than Epicurus' gods but as indolent, as impotent, while the boundless chaos of hunger and want welters terrific in its dark fury under their feet.
Ten years ago in the United States there were 2,352 people who paid an income tax on incomes acknowledged to be over $100,000 per year; last year that number had increased to 14,701. Ten years ago there were twenty-one people in the United States who paid an income tax on incomes of over $1,000,000 per year; last year there were 504. Ten years ago there were six people in the United States who paid an income tax on incomes acknowledged to be over $5,000,000 per year; last year there were thirty-six. The figures for Canada on incomes over $30,000 have trebled during the past three years, largely as a result of high tariffs.
How long are the great masses of the people going to stand for this sort of thing? As I

The Address-Mr. Brasset
said before, I am in sympathy with the amendment moved by the hon. member for Macleod. I believe that the government will have to take charge of the issuing of currency and establish a central bank of discount. The great masses of the people are no longer going to be trodden down under the iron heel of economic tyranny. How can the farmer pay off the liabilities he incurred five years ago when the price of grain and other products was so much higher than it is at the present time? Something will have to be done by the provincial governments in the matter of the readjustment of debts and after that is done the federal government will have to take control of the issuing of currency, establish a central bank of discount and remove all tariff barriers. When that is done the people of this country will be able to go along to a greater prosperity.
Til fares the land, to hast'ning ills a prey,
Where wealth accumulates and men decay;
Princes and lords may flourish, or may fade;
A breath can make them, as a breath has made:
But a bold peasantry, their country's pride.
When once destroy'd can never be supplied.
Mr. MAURICE BiRASSET (Gaspe) (Translation) : Mr. Speaker, I had not intended, at first to take part- in this debate, however, I deem it my duty to acquaint the house with my views on the subject matter, and which, I think, are shared by the majority of the people of this country, and especially those of my county.
I wish to appeal to the government on behalf of the Canadian people who have been in distress for more than two years. As the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Mar-cil) so eloquently put it, Canada has had to face many crises in the past. That of 1878 had been, up to this day, the greatest and longest which Canada had experienced; however, if we compare it with the one which has been prevailing for the last two years, the depression of 1878 is hardly worth mentioning. Throughout the whole country cries of distress and desolation are heard. Nobody works, nobody has any money. In all parts of the country, schools are closing their doors because the ratepayers cannot meet their taxes or the children find clothes to go to school. And who can tell what the coming winter has in store for us, the prognostics seem worse than those of the last two winters.
This session was called earlier than usual in order to consider the agreements concluded at the last Imperial economic conference. However, may I inform the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) and his cabinet that
53719-10*
they have to solve problems far more serious and urgent than the agreements entered into at the conference. Moreover, the Prime Minister informed us the other day, that the results of this conference would probably not be felt for two, three or four years. Must the people of this country still bear up with their sad lot for three or four years longer, before being relieved? Or is this statement of the Prime Minister simply a forerunner to prepare the people of Canada for a future statement admitting that the conference was a failure? Although I do not wish to doubt the sincerity of the Prime Minister, I fear, however, that the government itself does not anticipate from this famous conference all that the people of Canada are entitled to expect. But admitting that the Prime Minister is in earnest-which, again, I do not wish to doubt,-is it not a fact that he should adopt more efficacious measures to relieve immediately the distress of the masses?
At the election, in 1930, two years ago, the right hon. Prime Minister, gave many pledges, and it is on the strength of these that he assumed power. It is useless to mention them again here; they were repeated so often in the house that the people of this country are familiar with them all. However, he also stated that unemployment, as it existed in 1930, was a national calamity and it behooved the government alone to remedy such a state. Elect me to power, he stated and I shall see that unemployment ceases. There was, however, very little unemployment then in Canada, and conditions, if we contrast them with those existing today, were relatively prosperous. Almost every one had work, and even the unemployed could secure work at times. Farmers found a ready market for their products; and fishermen could dispose of their catch at a fair profit. Prices were high and the people, as a whole, were happy. Conservatives, however, described the situation in such gloomy terms, and the future, under a Conservative regime, in such bright colours, that the Canadian people were finally persuaded to enter into that famous Conservative paradise. We have now been in it for two years. What has been the result? The truth is that, in 1930, the country was far more prosperous than it is today. When the Bennett tariff, the so called protective tariff, was put into force, we witnessed trade decrease and industries totter. And now, owing to this exaggerated tariff, which has cut off our trade with foreign countries, the unemployment problem which, in 1930, was purely a local question, has become a national one: national because it has spread

The Address-Mr. Brasset
to all the provinces, national because it affects our trade and industries. It was not in 1930, that we needed a saviour but now that we need one. Yet, what is the right hon. Mr. Bennett's reply, when we beg of him to do something to relieve the distress of the people? He answers: the Dominion government has nothing to do with unemployment; this question must be settled by the provinces and provincial governments. The relief to the distress prevailing in this country is not within our jurisdiction; let the provinces look after it. We have more important questions to settle. We convened a great conference, which has brought much glory to our Prime Minister, and we wish above all to have these pacts approved, even should the results not be apparent before three or four years. The Canadians are of little importance, our conference takes precedence. Is that, sir, the realization of the pledges given by the Prime Minister, two years ago?

In fact, this famous conference, even were [DOT]4 to give us tangible results-which I do not think-amounts to a series of treaties. If these treaties are to relieve the situation, why then did the government not apply itself to this task long before today, in 1930, for instance? For it is not necessary to convene an Imperial conference in order to negotiate pacts with the various parts of the empire. These pacts could have been agreed upon long ago and they would be in force today, without having to gather here all the delegates of the commonwealth, including an army of secretaries, assistant secretaries, agents, etc., etc., brought here at the expense of the country- at an enormous expense. The Prime Minister has laid on the table of the house the various agreements entered into. They will be discussed next week, by those better posted than I am. May I simply point out that they will in no way activate the trade in Canada; the effect will be to displace this trade to the benefit of the empire, but to the detriment of certain other countries. I wonder what has become of the famous motto "Canada First" which was one of the fundamental articles of the Conservative program in 1930. Canada will not increase her trade by one cent; instead of trading with France and the United States, we shall almost drain the sources of this country's trade in favour of the empire.
I read this evening in the Le Droit, an article which is as follows:
Washington 13	(P.C.).-United States exports to Canada may be reduced annually by about $75,000,000 as a result of the higher tariff rates on non-British products made effective in the Dominion under Imperial
[Mr. Brasset. 1
conference agreements. This is under the assumption that empire exporters will take full advantages of the increased preferences accorded them and that the United States producers will be unable to overcome the handicap by lowering the cost of production and other means. This estimate was agreed upon in informed circles here after a partial analysis of information received from the American legation at Ottawa as to the commodities affected by the agreements.
In nearly all discussions on the effect of the tariff changes on American trade, it is emphasized that the 1930 exports to Canada of $660,000,000 represent more closely "normal trade" than the $902,000,000 of 1929. Last year's exports totalling $395,647,000 are similarly regarded as sub-normal; likewise the low level of the current year's shipments. Exports to Canada in the first 8 months of 1932 were valued at $170,432,000 compared with $295,701,000 in the corresponding period last year, and $480,357,556 in the first eight months of 1930.
Then, sir, the loss we sustain in exports to the United States we will gain with the empire, but this will not be a favourable change for Canada, it will simply mean a displacement of Canada's trade.
There will, sir, soon be an election in the neighbouring republic. If, as everything leads us to believe the Republicans lose this election and the Democrats win, the latter will probably approach us and offer us terms which I suppose will be advantageous to us.
In fact, Mr. Roosevelt, the Democratic candidate, recently made the statement that if he were elected president of the United States, he intended to give his country a period of Liberalism. The following is a despatch from Denver, Colorado, dated September 16, last:
Mr. Franklin D. Roosevelt stated last night in the course of an improvised speech delivered before a group of democratic leaders of Colorado, that if the government of the State of New York, had been in the hands of the democratic party for twelve out of the last fourteen years, it was that "under the direction of Alfred Smith it looked after the welfare of the citizens." The democratic candidate to the presidency added that the country was entering into a new era of liberalism.
If then, according to the statement of the Democratic candidate to the United States presidency, that country makes reasonable offers to us, we will be tied down for five years with the various parts of the British commonwealth, and therefore unable to take advantage of the Democratic offer. It will not be possible for us to return to a moderate tariff, we shall have to suffer the consequences, and even if other countries, realizing the futility of exaggerated protection, return to a better conception of their interests, we shall be unable to follow their example, tied down,

The Address-Mr. Brasset
sewn, as it were, in the folds of a treaty which we will be unable to cancel for a number of years. I contend, sir, that this is unfair to Canada. The Canadian people have suffered enough without forcing them to bear another ordeal.

The Conservative government has often proclaimed that a high protective tariff was the panacea which would cure all ills, all the wounds of Canada. How can we explain then that the number of unemployed which amounted to only 250,000 in 1930, has reached 800,000 in 1932. This number does not include bank and shop clerks, those that we designate as the white collar unemployed which also forms an interesting class.
How does it happen that our exports which amounted to $1,208,338,430 in 1930, had dwindled to $617,243,023 in 1931?
How can we explain that our national debt, after falling off yearly from 1924 to 1930, increased by $200,000 in 1931 and 1932?
How does it happen that Canada, after having had a steady yearly surplus from 1924 to 1930, has had to register two huge deficits in 1931 and 1932?
How can we explain that during the period when thrift was advised and thousands of Dominion employees were dismissed, the yearly expenditure was increased?
How does it happen that the right hon. Mr. Bennett, after having won his election on the New Zealand butter question, acknowledges today that it is necessary to import millions of pounds of butter from New Zealand?
How can we explain that Canadian butter which sold 35 cents per pound in 1930, only sells at 18, 20 or 22 cents today? How does it happen that the customs revenues which amounted to $200,000,000, in 1929, are only $113,000,000, in 1932, notwithstanding an increase in customs duties? How are we to explain that the industrial production of Canada, since 1929, has decreased about $700,000,000? Finally how can we explain that the returns of the Canadian National railways have decreased $90,000,000, in two years?
These questions and many others would need to be answered. If the government were to reply, it would be by one word: depression.
ho doubt, the world crisis has largely contributed to the fiasco of the government's policy, but it is also certain that the absurd customs measures, exaggerated duties and impediments to trade and industry, have also aggravated the situation, and if we find ourselves today, in distress, we must place the responsibility, to a great extent, on those who, in 1930, pledged themselves to put an end to all the ills we were suffering and lead us into paradise.
We still hear the voice of the right hon. Mr. Bennett from the top of hustings proclaiming that there was no need for a Canadian to suffer from unemployment and hunger.
This was in 1930, and the Conservatives might contend again that they could not then realize what the conditions would be in the country two years hence.
We are now, in 1932, after two years have elapsed of Conservative rule. The Conservatives know what they are doing, they know what has been the outcome of their policy, last year, therefore, to meet the deficits, to prevent a decrease in trade, they brought down the tariff of Hon. Mr. Rhodes. That famous tariff was to put an end to our deficits and give us surpluses. The Conservatives were not taken unawares and they cannot contend that they did not know what to expect. The following is what I find, in the Evening Citizen, dated October 14.
Rhodes' Budget Estimate Fails Government had hoped that $40,000,000 extra revenue would be forthcoming Lessened importation of foreign goods and a corresponding decline in customs duties are mainly responsible for the revenue situation disclosed in the monthly statement today. The total revenue of the department in the six months was $99,120,093. Customs declined by nearly nineteen millions and excise duties by over four millions, but, against this, excise taxes increased by nearly sixteen millions. The net decrease was therefore $7,856,175.
Income taxes in the six months brought in $51,587,611, an increase of $1,866,543.
September revenues, amounting to $16,088,443 reflect a net decrease of $2,324,288.
The figures are disappointing in view of the budget estimate of 40 millions of extra revenue.
That is, sir, the Conservative government thought that they had good grounds to believe that according to the budget brought down last year not only would there not be any deficit this year, but the government hoped for a surplus of $40,000,000 over the revenue of last year. Again, they were not taken unawares, they knew what awaited them: they reaped what they had sown. Instead of a $40,000,000 revenue, there is a $9,000,000 deficit, to date. This means further taxation.
1 wonder how the hon. Minister of Finance
The Address-Mr. Brasset

will levy these new taxes? We are overburdened with them, we do not know where to turn we have no income left because of the Conservative tariff. The hon. Minister of Finance will be forced to levy new taxes and the Canadians will have to hear the burden. There is a 4 per cent sales tax; a stamp tax and many more which the Conservative government conceived. Notwithstanding all this. We must be further taxed not only to cover the $7,000,000 deficit of last year, but also to find $40,000,000 of additional revenue that the Conservatives had expected to realize this year.
It is pitiful, sir.
Allow me to give a concrete example of the result of the high tariff existing in this country for the last two years, especially as to its effect on agriculture. A few years ago, in 1929, and even at the beginning of 1930, farmers could obtain about 18 to 19 cents per pound on raw hides. These hides were then manufactured and put on the market. Leather sold about 40 cents per pound. Today, owing to the general stagnation of trade, the farmers find no sale for raw hides, or when they do happen to dispose of them they are paid only 1 cent per pound. Leather nevertheless still retails at 40 cents per pound. That is to say, m 1930, the handling cost at the tannery, was 20 cents, while today it has risen to 39 cents. The farmer is the sufferer and the manufacturer, protected cut of all proportion by the government, benefits.
The same thing applies to marine motors, in which the people of my county, who are mostly fishermen, are especially interested. These motors which sold, let us say, $250 in
1929,	at the beginning of 1930, still sell at $250. But, sir, the price of steel and iron has dropped 100 per cent. The iron and steel workers earned then 5, 6 and 7 dollars per day, and today they are willing, when they get a job, to work for $2.50 or $3 per day. Therefore, marine motors which, in 1929 and
1930,	sold for $250 should sell, today, at the most $125. Who benefits by protection, if not the manufacturer, and who suffers, if not the farmer, the fisherman and the workman.
In 1921, Canada shipped to the United States $21,600,000 worth of live stock. In
1931,	owing to the Hawley-Smoot tariff, they only shipped $700,000. In 1921, Canada shipped $1,600,000 worth of sheep and in 1931, it shipped the enormous sum of $240,000, due to the tariff of S3 per head on cattle. As to butter, in 1921, Canada exported to the United States $101,000,000 worth, while, in 1931, our exports only amounted to $2,000,000. One may contend

that it was the United States which barred our exports by their prohibitive tariff. My reply is that we were not slow in adopting the Bennett tariff. As I stated a moment ago, when our neighbours are probably on the eve of returning to a moderate tariff, we jeopardize our chances; prosperity will return in their midst while we will be compelled to carry on with our high tariff, and, thereby, live in stagnation.
I might point out that the same thing applies to the French treaty which was abrogated by this government. We are often asked the question:	What would you,
Liberals, do to relieve the situation if your party was returned to power? I shall answer the question, sir, and then close my remarks. We would make no promises like the Conservatives did, in 1930, and as they do today with reference to the Imperial conference. Should we be returned to power, we would simply apply the tariff of moderate protection of that great Canadian, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who gave sixteen years of unprecedented prosperity to his country. We would apply the same policy followed by the Right Hon. Mackenzie King and which also gave the country ten years of prosperity. That is what the Liberals would do to promote the best interests of the Canadian people, and I trust it will be soon.

Not only have they not offered in the speech from the throne anything for the rural people or for the people of Canada as a whole, but when the farmers and the people of rural Canada come to see them they refuse to talk to them. No man, Mr. Speaker, whether he be prime minister or governor general or king, has a right to refuse to see such a delegation of people who are living under conditions which
are affecting not only their mentality but their health and the morale of their families. Truly I do not know how any member from the province of Manitoba, one of the banner provinces of this Dominion-these rural members especially-can sit behind a government, behind a prime minister, behind all the ministers who refused to go and listen to these serious-minded people.
I have an advantage, Mr. Speaker, over a good many hon. members in that I can read the speech from the throne in both languages. I have read it in both languages; I have studied it in both languages, and there is not a thing in it for the people of Canada except the report of the royal commission on transportation, and that report you might just as well throw to the winds because this present government has done everything in its power to ruin the Canadian National Railways.

And it is ruining the
morale of the employees of the Canadian National Railways. The other thing that I see in the speech from the throne is that the Bank Act will not be revised this year. When the farmers in my district, the farmers in all the districts of Manitoba who had their 150 or their 200 acres of land ready for the binder, went to the banks to borrow $25 or $30 to buy their twine, what did the bankers say to them? "How do you intend to pay that money back?" "By the revenues and profits from the operation of my farm." And the bankers say, "You know you can't do it." And the bankers were telling the truth. What did these people do? Took two or three milking cows that were giving the bare necessities of the family, put them into a truck, drove into the city of Winnipeg and sold them in order to buy twine to tie their grain that was lying out in the field. Yet this government offers the rural population of Canada a postponement of revision of the Bank Act when rural Canada and the whole of Canada is in need of credit facilities more than ever before. I am not criticizing the banks for not lending money to the farmer, but if the banks cannot or will not do it, then let the government establish some system of credit which will do it. This country cannot run without credit. If the government is not going to establish some system of credit, some means whereby a farmer will be able to get a few dollars in order to take off his crop, we might as well go home and tell the people what I told them during the campaign, that there is nothing this government has done since it has been in power that has not been detrimental to the
The Address-Mr. Beaubien

agricultural industry. And the people believed me: in two ridings in which I spoke, including my own federal riding, two candidates lost their deposits and the others got badly trimmed.

I made this statement
in regard to trade matters during the provincial campaign-

Don't change it.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Will my hon. friend
keep quiet?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
There are
just six Liberals in the house listening to you.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
My hon. friends opposite cannot listen while they are talking. If my hon. friend for Parkdale (Mr. Spence), instead of having a pen in his hand, would sit and listen to me, he would get something into his head, but you cannot get something into a man's head if he goes on writing all the time.
During the provincial compaign I made this statement, that every action of this federal government in regard to trade matters has been ruinous to the agricultural industry, and they know it themselves. We have recently had an Imperial economic conference. At that conference the British Empire had a chance to give the world a lead-and somebody has to give the world a lead.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: What about you?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I am giving it to you
if you would only listen. The bigger the man, the thicker the head.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
And the smaller the
man-?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I repeat that we recently had an Imperial economic conference, where an opportunity was afforded for the delegates from the different parts of the British Empire

to give the world a lead; and somebody has to give this world a lead in trade matters. But what did they do? They followed the very system which they have followed and which has ruined this and every other country in the world, which has increased unemployment by millions and millions, which has killed agriculture and all other primary industries, and which is ruining the secondary industries. I have gone through as many of the schedules as I possibly could. I confess I do not understand all of them, but I do know this, that the same fiscal policies which have been applied by the present government for two years are embodied in these conference agreements. Not only are they embodied in the agreements, but the country is being tied down to these agreements for five years. If within the next five years we want to change our tariff on any of the commodities mentioned in the agreements we cannot do it, because we have to maintain certain margins prescribed in the agreements. But what about our trade with the rest of the world? Do we not want to trade with the outside world? This government, not satisfied with putting a tariff wall around Canada and ruining our own country, are trying to ruin the whole British Empire by encircling it completely with a tariff wall. As a member of this house representing an agricultural constituency, and having the interests of the whole of Canada at heart, I am not going to swallow these trade agreements holus bolus just to please my right hon. friend the Prime Minister. The whole thing is a joke.
iSome hon. MEMBERS: Oh, oh.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: It is a joke; you know it is a joke, and you cannot get- away from it.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Sure.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The hon. member for
North Huron (Mr. Spotton)-it cannot be South Huron or my hon. friend would not have been in this house-knows that the very fiscal policy that has been followed by this government during the last two years, and has ruined this country, is embodied in these trade agreements. Take the preference on wheat, for instance. What does that give to the farmer? When Great Britain cannot consume our wheat, what will the other non-empire countries do if you put this wall around the empire? They will simply impose high tariffs against our wheat, to the disadvantage of the Canadian farmer. No, Mr. Speaker, in this country and in the whole world there has to be downward revision of tariffs. The world

Questions
has to get away from this self-contained nationalistic madness, and instead trade with one another.
My friends .to my left talk about a depreciated and an inflated currency. I know nothing about it, but if it is going bo remedy conditions, let us adopt some different system of credit facilities with a view to bringing about a better relationship between the price level of farm commodities and the price level of other goods. When this country comes back to normal conditions, when prosperity returns to Canada in any degree, it will come only when the agricultural industry is on a paying basis. It will come then and no sooner, and every member of this house knows it. You cannot tell me that you are going to put agriculture on a paying basis by raising tariff barriers, thus increasing the price of everything the farmer has to buy and increasing his production costs. How are you going to make agriculture prosperous? I am not looking for very much higher prices for cereals. I do nolt suppose that we will get very much higher prices for some years, but if this government had not come into power we would have had a narrower spread between the price of goods the farmer sells and the price of the goods he has to buy.
I cannot understand the attitude of my hon. friends on the other side of the house, sitting silent all through this debate, unless the explanation is that they are ashamed of the action of the government, that they are afraid to say anything for fear that they will pub their foot in iit. I have been a member of this house for eleven years. I have attended every session and have listened attentively to every debate on the address, but this is the first debate of importance that I have seen-and this debate is more important than any in the past because of the condition the country is ini-in which 135 members speak through the mouth of only one man, and themselves remain dumb throughout the whole debate.
On motion of Mr. Garland (Bow River) the debate was adjourned.
